name: Emeka Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent of AI firms, employers, unions, parties and government, and we don't sell anything or campaign. Your answers are confidential, including what you would say only in private. What does a normal workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I supervise four people who sort supplier invoices at a large furniture company's central office. I used to do the checking myself and got made a junior manager this year, so now I also handle the queue and the complaints when a supplier wasn't paid. I'm still slow with the monthly forecast; one of my team often catches a number I've missed.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What keeps you there, and what is difficult at home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like getting a small workshop paid before its owner has to ring twice. I'm 43, with a bachelor's degree, a mortgage, my wife Nia and our two children, aged nine and thirteen. Nia cleans at the local school on short hours, and my manager pay is at the lower end; after the boiler repair we have less than two weeks of expenses saved. There are few other offices like this nearby, and I have never used an AI tool because I don't trust a screen to explain a disputed bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If software only files the easy invoices, I expect the disputed ones to stay on our desks. I could keep learning this manager job. The boiler bill and mortgage don't vanish because AI turns out quiet, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team to keep reading the delivery note before approving a short payment. I'd tell Nia the desk probably stays much as it is. I wouldn't call the small filing tool a threat in front of the staff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm already worried about money. Two weeks of expenses won't carry a family through a missed pay cheque, and I don't feel quick at the forecast yet. AI staying small would stop one worry, not fix the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting Friday I'd sit with the senior clerk for one hour on this month's forecast, then ask her to check it with me before I send each later monthly report. Through the first year of a plateau I'd keep this post and stop our Saturday takeaway for three months, putting that money toward a 500 cash buffer. If the school cuts Nia's hours, we'd pay the mortgage first and ask the utility for a payment plan before a bill is overdue.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel worried despite the quiet AI picture. My family was already close to the edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the takeaway save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About 25 each Saturday. The children will complain for a week, then we'll cook together. I'm not taking their school meals away to make a point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask for help with the forecast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I already do, though I hate showing how much I need it. The senior clerk knows the supplier cycles better than I do. I'd rather ask her than send a wrong number and have four people carry it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Checking invoices, planning cash and answering suppliers is nearly the whole office. A stronger system could do the easy and hard cases faster than my team, while the loading crew is still carrying furniture by hand. I was the last manager promoted; that does not make me the last one kept.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff representatives for a meeting before the company changes the invoice queue. I'd tell my team they deserve to know which jobs could be cut and what paid training is offered. I would not promise that the warehouse can take everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my post could go, and Nia's school wage would not cover the mortgage by itself. A few local firms have accounts desks, but not enough for everyone leaving ours. I feel behind because I have never used AI, and the old forecasting work is what I am still learning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd ask the staff council to seek a written staffing plan and notice terms from the director. I'd keep working on the disputed invoices while the plan is argued, and I'd call our mortgage lender about its hardship process before any missed payment, without assuming we qualify. In the first year of rollout I'd apply for any posted invoice or stores-clerk vacancy that pays enough for the mortgage, but I wouldn't resign without an offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed. I could be the first manager the director decides she can do without.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the new software if the firm asked?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want a colleague to sit beside me on a test file with no real supplier details. I have never opened an AI tool and I won't pretend I can run one alone tomorrow. If the firm pays for proper time to learn, I'd try, but I wouldn't put a real bill through it unseen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children about the money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we might cook at home more and skip the spring trip. I wouldn't tell a nine-year-old the mortgage might fail when I still have a wage. Nia and I would make that call together if it came to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A system doing almost all thinking work by 2028 could check every invoice and answer every supplier. My office job may go then, not when robots start moving furniture around 2031. I don't have the money to spend two years exploring ten careers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the staff council we need dates, severance terms and a real appeal if an automatic payment harms a supplier. I'd tell Nia we must make a house plan before any notice arrives. Publicly I'd ask for income help for families whose work disappears, while admitting we would have to qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect my office role to end around 2028, and Nia's school wage is far below our mortgage and bills. We have less than two weeks saved, and only a few similar offices nearby. I'm frightened that the children will see us pack the house before I can find another wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this week Nia and I would call the lender to learn the exact hardship terms and ask her school whether more paid hours are available. I'd ask the staff council to demand a written notice period and redeployment vacancies, then stop the spring trip before paying its deposit. If AGI arrives in 2028 and my job ends, I'd apply for a posted warehouse receiving role only if it still needs people and its wage plus Nia's covers the mortgage and groceries; otherwise we'd ask family for a short loan only if they can spare it and check any public support eligibility before budgeting it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed, close to panicked. I have steps on paper, but almost no cash if those steps fail.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the warehouse receiving role survive until 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The physical counting and carrying might, but the ordering and paperwork could change in 2028. I can't say they will hire me just because the work exists. I'd need training and a wage offer before telling the children we're safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who in the family could lend, and for how long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My sister Ada has helped before, but she has children too. I'd ask for one mortgage instalment, with a repayment date, only if she says she can spare it. I would not build a whole year of spending on my sister's pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to find whether a paid move is possible before the invoice office faces AGI in 2031. Physical receiving still has until around 2034 before the robots in this picture can do it. I know the receiving desk's orders and reports could be automated in 2031, so a title there wouldn't protect us by itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the staff representatives to negotiate paid training into actual receiving vacancies now. I'd tell Nia we can try to add to savings before 2031, one pay period at a time. I wouldn't tell the children a course means a new wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might keep earning if the company has a receiving post with physical checks and trains me for it. I have not done that work, and a lower rate could still leave the mortgage short. Five years is more useful than two, but I can't pay for an unfunded course while the boiler bill is fresh.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next year I'd ask for one paid shadow shift a month in receiving, and if the supervisor approves I'd complete those shifts checking damaged boxes with an experienced worker. Nia and I would send 30 a week into a cash envelope whenever her school hours and my pay cover the mortgage and food. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, I'd apply only for a posted receiving vacancy whose wage plus Nia's covers those bills; if none opens, I'd seek written lender terms and search the few nearby employers while still on notice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious, though the five-year window gives me a little room. I still see the mortgage every time I close my eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in receiving besides watch?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check the delivery sheet against the actual boxes, flag damaged furniture and learn to use the safety gear. I'd need someone to show me the lift equipment before I touched it. I'm not going to become a warehouse expert by standing there once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How much could you really save?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirty a week when both pay cheques arrive, and zero when Nia's hours fall. That isn't a grand fund; it would cover a repair or a week of groceries. I'd rather say that than pretend we're building six months overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years sounds generous until I think our mortgage could still be due when the younger child is nineteen. The invoice office can still go in 2036, and physical warehouse work meets robots around 2039. I would have longer to pay down the mortgage and learn something else, but I start with almost no savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a large firm should offer paid training to the people whose office work it plans to remove. I'd ask the staff council to keep track of promised vacancies, not just course seats. I'd tell neighbours public help should cover families who cannot find a paid route, with proper rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might build a buffer and become a competent receiving worker before 2036, but that depends on paid shifts being available. I'm still the new manager here, and I don't want to lose ten years waiting for a promotion that may never come. Even a physical role could change when robots arrive in 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In 2027 I'd ask the receiving manager for a paid six-month rotation, and if approved I'd complete the supervised box and damage checks. I'd keep the Saturday takeaway cut and put 30 a week toward a one-month cash buffer whenever the mortgage and food are covered. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, I'd take a posted receiving job only if its pay with Nia's covers the mortgage and groceries; if it doesn't, I'd keep searching and ask the lender about any hardship option before an instalment is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the mortgage despite the time. Ten years helps only if we can keep earning through it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you pay down the mortgage faster in those years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not at the moment. I'd put a month of expenses away before making extra repayments. If Nia gets steady hours later, we could revisit the mortgage, but I won't spend money we haven't earned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why stay with the staff council rather than handle this alone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are four people reporting to me who earn less than I do. A written offer to one person doesn't tell us what happens to the others. I'd rather have the vacancy list on the table where everyone can see it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My new role is mostly checking and answering, and two years is less time than our mortgage term gives us to breathe. A written notice period, a paid route to a real job and a temporary mortgage arrangement if we qualified would help. I'd want the staff representatives at the table before jobs are announced away.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask the supplier waiting for payment what an automatic apology is worth. One cabinet maker told me his workers would miss Friday's wages if we held his invoice again. An automatic apology won't pay a cabinet maker's workers on Friday. I still hear his voice when the queue looks like rows on a screen.

headlineQuote: An automatic apology won't pay a cabinet maker's workers on Friday.
portrait: Emeka, **43**, became a junior invoice team manager this year after years of checking supplier bills at a large furniture company.
He is still learning forecasts, earns **low manager pay** and has under two weeks saved after a boiler repair.
His wife Nia works **short school-cleaning hours**; they have two school-age children and a mortgage, with few comparable offices nearby.
He has **never used AI** and seeks staff representation, paid openings and conditional mortgage help as his desk work faces change.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase his new office role before the family builds a cash buffer.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and paid training tied to an actual vacancy before wages end.
A **mortgage arrangement** only if the lender offers one and the family qualifies.
